name: journalctl
description: Queries the systemd journal: all system and service logs in one indexed, structured store.

flags.description: Logs of one service, e.g. -u nginx.
Logs of the current boot / previous boot.

examples.explanation: The last 50 log lines of nginx — the first command for any web server problem.
Live-follows nginx logs while you reproduce an issue.

examples.output: Jan 12 10:01:22 web01 sshd[2140]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7
examples.explanation: All errors from the last hour — here an SSH brute-force attempt is visible.
Logs from the PREVIOUS boot — essential after a crash or unexpected reboot.

examples.output: Archived and active journals take up 512.0M
examples.explanation: Checks journal disk consumption; cap it with --vacuum-size=200M.

about: The journal stores binary, structured logs in /var/log/journal/ (persistent if the directory exists) or /run/log/journal (volatile). journald indexes by boot, unit, priority, and time, making queries instant. Traditional plain-text logs in /var/log/syslog or /var/log/messages usually still exist in parallel.
useCases: Filter system-wide events by time and severity.
mistakes: Expecting persistence without configuring it: on some distros the journal is volatile by default (check /var/log/journal exists).
Searching with grep instead of journalctl matches — the built-in filters are indexed and faster.
warnings: journald rate-limits noisy services; a service's logs can be dropped silently — check journalctl -u UNIT for "Suppressed" messages.
distroNotes: systemd distributions only. Logs persist across reboots only when /var/log/journal exists (Storage=persistent in journald.conf).
